earlier_scan.source_named: Ekiugbo, Philip O. 2016. The sound system of Uvwie (full phonology, plausibly covers prosody). Ekiugbo & Ugorji 2019 (Lagos Linguistics Assoc., read online) covers vowels/tone only, no stress statement.

tone_statements.citation: Elugbe, Ben Ohiomamhe. 1989. Comparative Edoid: phonology and lexicon. Delta Series 6. Port Harcourt: University of Port Harcourt Press. 270 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Omamor (1973) marks only high and low on her Uvbie examples. I have myself not found cause to mark a third level. A non-low level (only a little higher than low) is heard at the end of utterances, but that may be due to the phenomenon of final low raising which is observable in most Edoid languages of the Delta.
tone_statements.check: quotation from the author's open copy, read 2026-09-25; not yet verified by a second reading

sources.citation: Ekiugbo, Philip Oghenesuowho & Christian Ugo Chukwunonye Ugorji. 2019. A Descriptive Phonology of the Vowel System of Uvwiẹ. Linguistique et Langues Africaines 5: 89-109. doi:10.4000/lla.760
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent. Vowel inventory, harmony, nasality, length; p.104: extra-short vowels only in initial onsetless low-toned syllables; long vowels only under 'derived contour tones — rising or falling', other vowels 'bear only register tones'. Vowel length not phonemic.

sources.citation: Ikoyo-Eweto, E. O. & Philip O. Ekiugbo. 2017. A phonetic analysis of Uvwiẹ vowels. Journal of West African Languages 44(2): 1-13.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-in
sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent. Acoustic vowel study (formants, duration); duration conditioned by tone and position (low-toned word-initial vowels shortest, contour-tone vowels longest, pp.7-8); 'vowel length is not phonemic in Uvwiẹ'.

sources.citation: Omamor, Augusta Phil. 1988. Okpe and Uvwiẹ: a case of vowel harmony galore. Journal of West African Languages 18(1): 47-64.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-in
sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent (scanned read in full). p.62 fn.5-6: tones marked High, Low and downstepped High (author unsure whether downstepped H or raised L); verbs carry no inherent tone in citation form, deriving tone from syntactic context 'as in most other Edoid languages'. Body discusses tonal patterns of tense forms, verbal nouns (LOW-HIGH, LOW-HIGH-LOW) and reduplications.
Consonant/vowel inventory only (citing Ekiugbo 2016, Omamor 1973, Archangeli & Pulleyblank 1994); nothing on tone or stress.

sources.citation: Ekiugbo, Philip Oghenesuowho. 2022. Rule Ordering in Uvwie. Macrolinguistics 10(1) [Serial No. 16]: 101-110. doi:10.26478/ja2022.10.16.4
sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent (0 hits). Treats Uvwie as tonal: level High and Low tones; rising/falling contour tones derived by 'tone fusion' of a floating tone after vowel elision, with vowel lengthening under contour tones (pp.106-108; abbreviations p.109 list High, Low, Rising, Falling Tone).

sources.citation: Omamor, Augusta Phil. 1986. Adjectives and adjectivalisation in some languages of the Western Delta of Nigeria. Journal of West African Languages 16(2): 9-26.
sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent (scanned, a full-text search for stress/accent + spot reading). Morphosyntax of quality verbs in Okpe and Uvwie; mentions only tonal shapes of reduplications (Uvwie type I LOW-HIGH-HIGH, type II LOW-HIGH-LOW-(LOW) with low-tone prefix u-).

sources.quote: Omamor (1973) marks only high and low on her Uvbie examples. I have myself not found cause to mark a third level. A non-low level (only a little higher than low) is heard at the end of utterances, but that may be due to the phenomenon of final low raising which is observable in most Edoid languages of the Delta.
sources.note: Per-language phonological summaries for all Edoid languages including Uvbiẹ; Elugbe's general statements on Edoid prosody (two basic tones, toneless verbs) and any remark on accent would apply; standard reference cited by every Uvwiẹ paper.
